content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer pZob (1/2)
content.comment:
We do appreciate your careful reviews and constructive comments. We dedicatedly tried our best to address your suggestions and concerns.

**[Q1]: I doubt the effect of the loss that pushes the feature with negative samples closer to the anchor feature. The combined feature of G and has only general information, but it doesn’t mean that the feature needs to be close to the negative feature. Please provide a more detailed explanation.**
 
[A1]:  Thank you for your great question. The motivation of the $\mathcal\{L\}^\{-\}_\{rcl\}$ is to push the negative samples closer to the anchor feature as well as to separate the positive samples from the anchor feature. Yes, actually there is no absolute need to push the negative samples closer to the anchor feature but we do need to separate the positive samples from the anchor feature. In this way, the positive samples could be well-separated from both negative samples and the anchor feature. In the experiments, results also show that loss $\mathcal\{L\}^\{-\}_\{rcl\}$ contributes much less than loss $\mathcal\{L\}^\{+\}_\{rcl\}$ but it can somehow prove that $\mathcal\{L\}^\{-\}_\{rcl\}$ does help. We further added more explanations in our updated draft.

**[Q2]: The ablation study is not sufficient. We cannot conclude from Table 4 that the instance normalization strategy is valid. More experiments are needed.**
 
[A2]: Thank you for constructive comments. We make more ablation studies of our method. Results are shown in the following Table. We consider  the 5 way 5 shot setting. GNN+IN indicates that we only employ the instance normalization strategy, w/o $\mathcal\{L\}^\{-\}_\{rcl\}$ indicates that we remove the $\mathcal\{L\}^\{-\}_\{rcl\}$ term, w/o $\mathcal\{L\}^\{+\}_\{rcl\}$ indicates that we remove the $\mathcal\{L\}^\{+\}_\{rcl\}$ term, and GNN+MemREIN w/o MB represents that we remove memory bank and directly use the feature map $D$. Comparing the results of Variant 1 and 2, it indicates that only applying the instance normalization operation results in the decrease of the accuracy. It is reasonable because the instance normalization operation will inevitably remove some discriminative useful information. In comparison with Variant 3 and 6, it validates the effectiveness of employing the memory bank on feature $D$.

 | 5 way 5 shot | Classification Accuracy (%) |             |             |               |             |   |
|--------------|:---------------------------:|:-----------:|:-----------:|:-------------:|:-----------:|---|
| ID           | Method                      | CUB         | Cars        | Places        | Plantae     |   |
| 1            | GNN                         | 69.26±0.68% | 48.91±0.67% | 72.59±0.67%   | 58.36±0.68% |   |
| 2            | GNN+IN                      | 67.34±0.66% | 42.76±0.75% | 67.82±0.73%   | 54.04±0.69% |   |
| 3            | GNN+MemREIN                 | **77.54±0.62%** | **56.78±0.66%** | **78.84±0.66%**   | **65.44±0.64%** |   |
| 4            | w/o$L_\{rcl\}^\{-\}$            | 75.38±0.63% | 55.34±0.72% | 78.03±0.68%   | 65.22±0.64% |   |
| 5            | w/o$L_\{rcl\}^\{+\}$            | 73.02±0.62% | 51.45±0.64% | 73.26±0.66%   | 62.22±0.64% |   |
| 6            | GNN+MemREIN w/o MB          | 75.98±0.62% | 54.64±0.66% | 74.86±0.68%   | 64.08±0.68% |   |

**[Q3]: Why does the model need to obtain R via a residual structure? If you want to distill and purify the discriminative information, the feature F is enough.** 
 
[A3]: Thank you for your  great question. We first pass $F$ through the instance normalization layer to get the feature $\widetilde{F}$ and then obtain feature $R$ via $F$ minus $\widetilde{F}$. 
 
The purpose of our model is to enhance the generalization ability of the model thus we employ the instance normalization to first reduce the instance-specific style discrepancy to help learn the domain-invariant features. The feature $R$ denotes the difference between the original input feature $F$ and the normalized feature $\widetilde{F}$. The reason that we use the residual structure is that residual operation can decrease the mean of the feature, which helps to improve the training and enhance the robustness. In addition, using residual feature instead of original feature is applied in many applications, i.e., motion prediction[1], trajectory prediction[2] and so on. 
 
[1] Dang, Lingwei, et al. "MSR-GCN: Multi-Scale Residual Graph Convolution Networks for Human Motion Prediction," ICCV, 2021.  
[2] Mohamed, Abduallah, et al. "Social-stgcnn: A social spatio-temporal graph convolutional neural network for human trajectory prediction," CVPR. 2020.

**[Q4]: There is a lack of experiments to prove the validity of memory bank. If there is no concatenation operation, is it valid to use D directly? (Eq. 8)**
 
[A4]: Thank you for your great suggestion. Experimentally, when applying the memory bank on the feature $D$ and directly using feature $G$ has the best performance.

Experimentally, when applying the memory bank on the feature $D$ and directly using feature $G$ has the best performance. content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a general framework, MemREIN, for cross-domain few-shot learning. It utilizes instance normalization and memorized restitution to strength the discrimination ability. In addition, the authors propose a novel reverse contrastive learning strategy to stabilize the distillation process. The experiment is sufficient and shows a significant improvement compared with state-of-the-art baselines for cross-domain few-shot learning, and gets comparable results to the best method for normal few-shot learning.
content.main_review:
The paper has the following strengths:
1.	The proposed method is a universal and method-agnostic module, which can be inserted to existing metric-based methods for cross-domain few-shot learning.
2.	The method uses instance normalization to alleviate the discrepancy across training sample, and design a memorized restitution module to adaptively distill the long-term fine-grained distinctive knowledge.
3.	A novel reverse contrastive learning strategy is proposed to disentangle general feature and discriminative feature. In this part, authors define reverse contrastive loss which makes anchor feature close to positive samples feature and separate from negative samples feature. 
4.	Extensive experiments on five popular benchmark datasets demonstrate that MemREIN well addresses cross-domain few-shot challenge.

There are some weaknesses:
1.	The differences of the proposed instance normalization from other normalization methods, such as batch/group/layer normalization, should be explained in detail. What’s more, its advantages should be elaborated.
2.	The memorized restitution sounds to be the most important contribution of the proposed method. For memorized restitution, why not consider to combine general feature map G with a memory bank? On the other hand, as D is updated with a memory vector, G can be computed as R - the updated D. Please clarify the logic behind using current G. 
3.	It would be better if more information about memory vector M is provided. To be specific, what is the relation between M and D in multiple iterations?
4.	In Table 2, under the leave one out setting the proposed method only be compared to “+LFP”. As ATA is a bit better than FP according to the results in Table 1, it would be more convincing to also including it in the comparison.
5.	The ablation study is helpful to check the significance of each module. It would be better to also show the results of w/o memory bank and w/o restitution.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new framework which is universal and method-agnostic, and conducts sufficient experiments. However, the novelty of the paper is not that significant, as the methods described in this paper are a little reproducible in prior works. The design of the modules is empirical, while more solid theoretical proof should be considered.

content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer jpdN (1/3)
content.comment:
We do appreciate your careful reviews and constructive comments. We dedicatedly tried our best to address your suggestions and concerns.

**[Q1]: The differences of the proposed instance normalization from other normalization methods, such as batch/group/layer normalization, should be explained in detail. What’s more, its advantages should be elaborated.** 
 
[A1]: Thank you for your constructive comments. Normalization has always been an active area of research in deep learning. It normalizes each feature so that it maintains the contribution of every feature, as some features have higher numerical value than others. This way the network can be unbiased (to higher value features). It also reduces internal covariate shift, which helps to improve the training.
 
For batch normalization [1], it computes the mean and variance of that feature in the mini-batch. It then subtracts the mean and divides the feature by its mini-batch standard deviation.  For layer normalization [2], it normalizes input across the features instead of normalizing input features across the batch dimension in batch normalization.
 
Actually, layer normalization and instance normalization are very similar to each other but the difference between them is that instance normalization normalizes across each channel in each training example instead of normalizing across input features in a training example. This technique was originally devised for style transfer [4][5][6], the problem instance normalization tries to address is that the network should be agnostic to the contrast of the original image. Group normalization [7]normalizes over a group of channels for each training example. 
 
We apply the instance normalization (IN) in our method because IN can reduce the instance-specific style discrepancy and help learn the domain-invariant features. Utilizing IN can enhance the model generalisation ability, which is what we tend to do. In addition, work [4] has experimentally shown that IN has more profound impacts than a simple contrast normalization.
 
 
[1] Ioffe, Sergey, and Christian Szegedy. "Batch normalization: Accelerating deep network training by reducing internal covariate shift." PMLR, 2015.  
[2] Ba, Jimmy Lei, Jamie Ryan Kiros, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. "Layer normalization." arXiv preprint arXiv:1607.06450, 2016.  
[3] Ulyanov, Dmitry, Andrea Vedaldi, and Victor Lempitsky. "Instance normalization: The missing ingredient for fast stylization." arXiv preprint arXiv:1607.08022, 2016.  
[4] Huang, Xun, and Serge Belongie. "Arbitrary style transfer in real-time with adaptive instance normalization." ICCV, 2017.  
[5] D. Ulyanov, A. Vedaldi, and V. Lempitsky, “Improved texture networks: Maximizing quality and diversity in feed-forward stylization and texture synthesis.” CVPR, 2017.  
[6] V. Dumoulin, J. Shlens, and M. Kudlur, “A learned representation for artistic style.” ICLR, 2017.  
[7] Wu, Yuxin, and Kaiming He. "Group normalization." ECCV, 2018.

content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer jpdN (2/3)
content.comment:
**[Q2]: The memorized restitution sounds to be the most important contribution of the proposed method. For memorized restitution, why not consider to combine general feature map G with a memory bank? On the other hand, as D is updated with a memory vector, G can be computed as R - the updated D. Please clarify the logic behind using current G.**

[A2]: Thank you for your great suggestion. The reason that we use the memory bank is that it is highly possible that the model would overfit because there are limited labeled samples under the few-shot learning framework, especially when we consider $D$ as relatively discriminative, and the memory bank has the smoothing effect. But for feature G, actually we don’t want this feature map to be smoothed since it is relatively general. Experimentally, when applying the memory bank on the feature $D$ and directly using feature $G$ has the best performance.
 
Experimental results of different ‘memory’ strategies are shown in the following Table. GNN+MemREIN w/o MB represents that we don’t use the memory bank neither on D nor G, GNN+MemREIN (on D) is our proposed method in which memory bank is operated only on D, GNN+MemREIN (on  D&G) represents that the memory bank is operated both on feature D and G (not shared). When the memory bank is operated on G, the performance drops.  Comparing these results, it indicates that when employing memory bank on feature $G$, it would cause performance decrease. Experimentally, when applying the memory bank on the feature $D$ and directly using feature $G$ has the best performance. Due to page limit, we update this part of results and discussion in the Appendix D.

|     5 way 5 shot     | Classification Accuracy (%) |             |               |             |
|:--------------------:|:---------------------------:|:-----------:|:-------------:|:-----------:|
|        Method        | CUB                         | Cars        | Places        | Plantae     |
| GNN+MemREIN (on D)   | **77.54±0.62%** | **56.78±0.66%** | **78.84±0.66%**   | **65.44±0.64%** |
| GNN+MemREIN w/o MB   | 75.98±0.62% | 54.64±0.66% | 74.86±0.68%   | 64.08±0.68% |
| GNN+MemREIN (on D&G) | 76.02±0.66% |  55.26±0.69% | 78.08±0.66%   | 64.84±0.68% |


**[Q3]: It would be better if more information about memory vector M is provided. To be specific, what is the relation between M and D in multiple iterations?** 
 
[A3]: Thank you for your great suggestion and sorry for the confusion about the update process of the memory bank, we further clarified this process in the updated draft. We update the memory bank as the follows:
 
$D^{l}(k,:,:) = maxpooling (concat(M^{(l)}_k,D(k,:,:)))$  
$M^{(l+1)}(k)=D^{l}(k,:,:)$  
where (l) represents the $l^{th}$ iteration, k represents the $k^{th}$ channel. 
 
After multiple iterations, the $M$ can be considered as a vector that stores the long-term information of feature $D$. 


**[Q4]: In Table 2, under the leave one out setting the proposed method only be compared to “+LFP”. As ATA is a bit better than FP according to the results in Table 1, it would be more convincing to also including it in the comparison.**
 
[A4]: Thank you for your great suggestion. We didn’t compare with + ATA under the leave one out setting because there is no result under this setting reported in their paper. We just noticed that they have released their codes. We are running their codes now and will definitely provide the results under this setting. We have discussed this great work and highlight its contributions in our updated draft  in the Related Work Section.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a cross-domain few-shot learning method, namely MemREIN, which consists of Instance Normalization and Memorized Restitution modules. An instance normalization layer is proposed to reduce the feature discrepancy between samples and enhance the overall generalization ability. A memorized restitution module is utilized to distill fine-grained discriminative knowledge about categories from the filtered out features. Beisdes, a reverse contrastive loss which encourages the further disentanglement of discriminative features and general features is proposed to stabilize the distillation process. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art approaches.
content.main_review:
Strength: The proposed MemREIN method is simple yet effective. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, the improvement of performance is significant.

Weakness:
1. Some explanations and descriptions of the method are unclear and insufficient. For example,  why use the memorized mechanism in the memorized restitution module? And how to update the memory vector "M"?
2. The ablation study is not very sufficient. There is a lack of the experiment verifing effectiveness of the memory bank in the memorized restitution module, which is an important term in the paper title.
3. Although the instance normalization layer is proposed to enhance the generalization ability, the ablation study in Table4,7 doesn't verify the effectiveness of it and the performance of "GNN+IN" is even worse. How about just using original feature F to obtain D and G? It seems that there should be an experiment about "GNN+MemREIN w/o IN" .
content.summary_of_the_review:
The MemREIN method proposed in this paper is simple and significantly improves the performance. But some explanations and descriptions about the memorized mechanism are unclear and insufficient. The corresponding ablation study is also lacking. More sufficient experiments should be included, e.g., verifying the effectiveness of the instance normalization layer. I would like to see the detailed response to my concerns in the rebuttal.

Updates: Although the authors address some of my concerns in the rebuttal, the question about  the effectiveness of the instance normalization layer still remains. So I would like to keep my current score.

replying_to: Replying to MemREIN: Rein the Domain Shift for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper3754 by Reviewer LXAQ

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a modular approach to boost performance for both cross-domain few-shot learning (CDFSL) and traditional few-shot learning (FSL). The modular approach involves applying the MemREIN module at the outputs of residual blocks. The MemReIN module includes an instance normalization layer followed by a disentanglement step. The disentanglement step involves extracting discriminative features from the residual of the instance normalized features by training a reverse contrastive loss. Results show substantial improvement in recognition performance for both CDFSL and FSL.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

- The concept of memorized restitution and reverse contrastive loss is novel in the context of CDFSL.

- The comparison studies are quite extensive both with CDFSL and traditional FSL although the dataset benchmark might be an issue.

- Results show significant improvement in recognition performance.


Weaknesses:

- The ability to generalize across domains has only been demonstrated over relatively small domain disparities e.g. compared to that present in the BCDFSL [1] setting which consists of large domain shift between natural images and satellite/ medical images. The current benchmark only considers natural images.

- The authors could discuss related work on the topic of partial/open-set/universal domain adaptation that does not assume that the source and target categories are the same and hence different from traditional domain adaptation. Also related work (just mentioning only published ones in main venues) on other recent works [2-6] on CDFSL should be compared/mentioned, even though some of them have been evaluated on a different benchmark. More importantly, it would be great to have a separate related work sub-section on cross domain few-shot learning. If space is an issue, domain generalization and traditional few-shot learning sections can be reduced since they are already well known by  the community.

- It seems that the exact method of normalization and restitution is already used in person re-identification but the authors do not refer the paper [7]. If one goes into the details of [7], the contribution of this paper seems to be very minor.

- The authors claim “instance normalization inevitably removes some discriminative information from the original feature maps ...”.  It would be great if authors mention some related work that shows that this is the case.

- “SE-like channel attention”. The Squeeze and Excite paper should also be referred here.

- I think there is lack of clarity in how the training and testing is taking place. How the memory restitution is done and how do you do forward and backward passes for reverse contrastive losses and how is batch-sampling done ? To address this, the authors could have an algorithm block (maybe in the supplementary material) to explain the complete training and testing process.

- Hyper-parameter sensitivity of lambda should also be carried out.

- The authors could do with a visualization of “important” and “contaminated” features maybe through T-SNE or feature maps that highlights the discriminability difference and disentanglement of the two feature types.

- Some design choices could be better justified maybe through experiments or theoretically:  Why the MemREIN blocks are applied after the last batch normalization layer of all the residual blocks and not every layer and not some layers ? Why avg pooling is used in Eq. (6) and max pooling in Eq. (8) ? What is the memory limit of the memory bank - is there any method to replace and store feature maps ?

- The authors could describe some limitations of their method: E.g. Can this MemREIN module be applied if we just have access to a source trained model without having access to source dataset for training ?

References:

[2] Zou, Yixiong, et al. "Revisiting Mid-Level Patterns for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Recognition." ACM Multimedia, 2021.

[7] Jin, Xin, et al. "Style normalization and restitution for generalizable person re-identification." CVPR, 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the idea is novel only in the context of CDFSL but it has been previously explored for person re-identification. Another major downside is that the method does not  demonstrate generalization across bigger domain disparities like the BCDFSL benchmark, which has large domain shifts between source and target categories.

-------- POST REBUTTAL ---------

The authors address some of my concerns about the paper. However, the concerns about novelty of the idea, evaluation on BCDFSL benchmark with recent approaches [2-6] and alternative model choices still remain. Hence, I would like to keep my current score.

We do appreciate your careful reviews and constructive comments. We dedicatedly tried our best to address your suggestions and concerns.

**[Q1]:  The ability to generalize across domains has only been demonstrated over relatively small domain disparities e.g. compared to that present in the BCDFSL [1] setting which consists of large domain shift between natural images and satellite/ medical images. The current benchmark only considers natural images.**
 
[A1]: Thank you for your good suggestion.  We are now extending our method to more benchmarks and will definitely provide the results under these benchmarks [1]. Based on our current experience and considering our results under the leave one out setting, when selecting one dataset as the target domain and combing other remaining datasets as the source domains, the scale and the diversity of the data becomes larger and the domain shift becomes large. We think our proposed method is still robust under other benchmarks
 
[1] Guo, Yunhui, et al. "A broader study of cross-domain few-shot learning." ECCV, 2020.

**[Q2]:  The authors could discuss related work on the topic of partial/open-set/universal domain adaptation that does not assume that the source and target categories are the same and hence different from traditional domain adaptation. Also related work (just mentioning only published ones in main venues) on other recent works [2-6] on CDFSL should be compared/mentioned, even though some of them have been evaluated on a different benchmark. More importantly, it would be great to have a separate related work sub-section on cross domain few-shot learning. If space is an issue, domain generalization and traditional few-shot learning sections can be reduced since they are already well known by the community.**
 
[A2]: Thank you for your good suggestion. We have added more related work about partial/open-set/universal domain adaptation and reduced the domain generalization part in our updated draft. In addition, there are great works[2-6] that have achieved promising performance in the cross-domain few-shot learning task. 
 
Specifically, Paper [2] studied a challenging subset of CDFSL where the novel classes are in distant domains from base classes. A residual-prediction task is proposed to encourage mid-level features to learn discriminative information of each sample to further boost the discriminability of mid-level features. 
 
Paper [3] presented a simple and effective solution to tackle this extreme domain gap: self-training a source domain representation on unlabeled data from the target domain. 
 
Paper [4] proposed a noise-enhanced supervised auto-encoder method to obtain the broader variations of the feature distributions to greatly boost the generalization capability of the model. 
 
Paper [5] tackled the problem of cross-domain few-shot learning where there is a large shift between the base and target domain using self-training. It proposed a simple dynamic distillation-based approach to facilitate unlabeled images from the novel/base dataset. 
 
Paper [6] proposed an effective mix-up module into the meta-learning mechanism and a novel disentangle module with a domain classifier to obtain domain-irrelevant and domain-specific features, which achieves promising performance. We further discussed and highlighted these great works in the Related Work Section in our updated draft.
 
[2] Zou, Yixiong, et al. "Revisiting Mid-Level Patterns for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Recognition." ACM Multimedia, 2021.  
[3] Phoo, Cheng Perng, and Bharath Hariharan. "Self-training for few-shot transfer across extreme task differences." ICLR, 2021.  
[4] Liang, Hanwen, et al. "Boosting the Generalization Capability in Cross-Domain Few-shot Learning via Noise-enhanced Supervised Autoencoder." ICCV, 2021.  
[5] Islam, Ashraful, et al. "Dynamic Distillation Network for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Recognition with Unlabeled Data." NeurIPS, 2021.  
[6] Fu, Yuqian, Yanwei Fu, and Yu-Gang Jiang. "Meta-FDMixup: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning Guided by Labeled Target Data." ACM Multimedia, 2021.

content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer LXAQ (2/3)
content.comment:
**[Q3]:  It seems that the exact method of normalization and restitution is already used in person re-identification but the authors do not refer the paper [7]. If one goes into the details of [7], the contribution of this paper seems to be very minor.**
 
[A3]: Thank you for your frank comment. Instance normalization is a well-studied strategy that has many applications. Paper [7] applied instance normalization operation in the person re-id task, this paper proposed an entropy based approach for feature purification. Differently, in our work, we first explore this instance normalization operation in the cross-domain few-shot learning task. We propose a novel memorized restitution approach to restitute the discrimination ability from the learned knowledge and we also propose a novel reverse contrastive loss to stabilize the distillation process, which are different from the orginal work. We would appreciate it if the reviewer can recognize our contributions.
 
[7] Jin, Xin, et al. "Style normalization and restitution for generalizable person re-identification." CVPR, 2020.  

**[Q4]:  The authors claim “instance normalization inevitably removes some discriminative information from the original feature maps ...”. It would be great if authors mention some related work that shows that this is the case.**
 
[A4]: Thank you for your good suggestion. We further added discussions in our updated draft about this case in Section 3.2.1. Specifically, “Instance  normalization  was originally used in style transfer (Dumoulin et al., 2016; Ulyanov et al., 2016; Huang & Belongie,2017), which is helpful to enhance the generalization ability by reducing the feature dissimilarity. Itcan remove instance/sample specific features out of the input, which makes more general featuresremained (Shankar et al., 2018; Volpi et al., 2018).However,  instance normalization inevitably removes some discriminative information from theoriginal feature maps (Jin et al., 2020; 2021),  which weakens the discrimination ability of theextracted features.”

**[Q5]:  “SE-like channel attention”. The Squeeze and Excite paper should also be referred here.**
 
[A5]: Thank you for your good suggestion. We further updated our draft in Section 3.2.2. Specifically, paper [8] proposed a SE-like channel attention that is able to adaptively recalibrate channel-wise feature responses by explicitly modelling interdependencies between channels
 
[8] Hu, Jie et. al. “Squeeze-and-excitation networks.” CVPR, 2018.

**[Q6]:  I think there is lack of clarity in how the training and testing is taking place. How the memory restitution is done and how do you do forward and backward passes for reverse contrastive losses and how is batch-sampling done? To address this, the authors could have an algorithm block (maybe in the supplementary material) to explain the complete training and testing process.**
 
[A6]: Thank you for your good suggestion. We further added more details in the updated draft and we will further draw an algorithm block for clear demonstration. In the training phase, we set $\lambda=0.1$ and train 1000 trials for all the methods. In each trial, we randomly sample $N_{w}$ categories with $N_{s}$ randomly selected images for each support set, and $16$ images for the query set. We use the Adam optimizer with the learning rate $0.001$. We further clarified the updating process of the memory bank in Section 3.2.2 and the process of reverse contrastive losses as well as batch-sampling in Section 3.2.3.

**[Q7]:  Hyper-parameter sensitivity of lambda should also be carried out.**
 
[A7]: Thank you for your good suggestion. We make the hyper-parameter study of $\lambda$ and results are shown in the following Table. We take the 5 way 5 shot setting with four different values of $\lambda={0.01,0.1,0.5}$. It can be observed that when setting $\lambda=0.1$, our method can achieve the best performance.  Due to page limit, we update this part of results and discussion in the Appendix E.

|  $\lambda=0.1$ |   |         **77.54±0.62%**         | **56.78±0.66%** |
|  $\lambda=0.5$ |   |         77.34±0.62%         | 56.66±0.66% |

**[Q8]:  The authors could do with a visualization of “important” and “contaminated” features maybe through T-SNE or feature maps that highlights the discriminability difference and disentanglement of the two feature types.**
 
[A8]: Thank you for your good suggestion. Quantitative results in Appendix D indicate the effectiveness of our proposed method of disentanglement of the important and contaminated features. We will further add more t-SNE examples to further show the difference of these two feature types.

content.title: Rebuttal to Reviewer LXAQ (3/3)
content.comment:
**[Q9]:  Some design choices could be better justified maybe through experiments or theoretically: Why the MemREIN blocks are applied after the last batch normalization layer of all the residual blocks and not every layer and not some layers? Why avg pooling is used in Eq. (6) and max pooling in Eq. (8)? What is the memory limit of the memory bank - is there any method to replace and store feature maps?**
 
[Q9]:  Some design choices could be better justified maybe through experiments or theoretically: Why the MemREIN blocks are applied after the last batch normalization layer of all the residual blocks and not every layer and not some layers? Why avg pooling is used in Eq. (6) and max pooling in Eq. (8)? What is the memory limit of the memory bank - is there any method to replace and store feature maps? 
 
[A9]: Thank you for your good question. We inserted MemREIN blocks after the batch normalization layer because our proposed method is operated on the feature-level and features that have passed though BN have small internal covariate shifts which is beneficial for training and convergence [9]. In addition, the CNN+BN structure is well applied and we don’t want to break this structure. We will provide more experiments on different strategies of the inserted position.  
 
We use average pooling in Eq.(6) because the SE-channel attention [8] uses global average pooling to generate channel-wise statistics to mitigate this problem that feature unit is unable to exploit contextual information outside of this region. We use max pooling in Eq.(8) because we aim to reserve the most discriminative information from the whole iteration process.
 
We update the memory bank as follows:  
$D^{l}(k,:,:) = maxpooling (concat(M^{(l)}_k,D(k,:,:)))$  
$M^{(l+1)}(k)=D^{l}(k,:,:)$  
where (l) represents the $l^{th}$ iteration, k represents the $k^{th}$ channel. 
 
The memory limit is actually the size of the feature $D$. Actually, there may be some other methods that can replace and store features such as the teacher-student model or asynchronous update strategy. The memory bank approach is a simple but effective approach
 
[8]  Hu, Jie et. al. “Squeeze-and-excitation networks.” CVPR, 2018.  
[9] Ioffe, Sergey, and Christian Szegedy. "Batch normalization: Accelerating deep network training by reducing internal covariate shift." PMLR, 2015.

**[Q10]:  The authors could describe some limitations of their method: E.g. Can this MemREIN module be applied if we just have access to a source trained model without having access to source dataset for training?**  
 
[A10]: Thank you for your good suggestion. Actually we don’t think our method can be applied if we just have access to a source trained model without having access to the source dataset for training. It is more like the source-free setting in the domain adaptation field and our method needs the source data for learning.
 
Thanks again for your careful reviews and valuable comments. We believe we have addressed most of your concerns. If you have further questions, feel free to ask and we are willing to have futher discussions with you.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a novel framework, MemREIN, which considers Memorized, Restitution, and Instance Normalization for cross-domain few-shot learning. An instance normalization algorithm is explored to alleviate feature dissimilarity, which provides the initial model generalization ability. A memorized module is further proposed to separate the most refined knowledge and remember it. A novel reverse contrastive learning strategy is proposed to stabilize the distillation process. Extensive experiments on five popular benchmark datasets demonstrate that MemREIN well addresses the domain shift challenge, and significantly improves the performance up to 16:37% compared with state-of-the-art baselines.
content.main_review:
++   The motivation of this paper is very clear.

++   Overall, the paper is well written. In particular, the METHOD section has a nice flow. Despite the method having limited novelty, the overall method is clearly described.

Concerns: 
 - Cross-domain few-shot learning has been studied a bit, and this paper does not give a corresponding presentation in the INTRODUCTION and RELATED WORK.
 - The main problem of the paper is the lack of rigorous experiments to study the usefulness of the proposed method. Although the paper does comparison experiments with more methods, the comparison methods used are not convincing enough for the effectiveness of the method proposed in the paper. It would be better if other methods from 2021 were included as comparison methods, such as:

[1] Hanwen Liang, Qiong Zhang, Peng Dai, Juwei Lu. Boosting the Generalization Capability in Cross-Domain Few-shot Learning via Noise-enhanced Supervised Autoencoder, In CVPR, 2021.

[2] Yuqian Fu, Yanwei Fu, Yu-Gang Jiang. Meta-FDMixup: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning Guided by Labeled Target Data. ACM Multimedia, 2021: 5326-5334.

 - For the results section, hyperparameter adjustment processes are not given. 

 - In addition to this, the tSNE visualization comparison (see Supplementary Material) mentions that the proposed method forms clear clusters of different classes compared to the previous methods. However, the improvement is not so obvious in Figure(f) with respect to Figure (d).

 Minor comments: 
* In the 4th line in 2.1 FEW-SHOT CLASSIFICATION, it should be "encodes" instead of "encode". In the page 6, it should be " defined in " instead of " defined is ".

* The flowchart of the overall algorithm should be refined a bit more as possible. 

Updates:
After reading the comments from other reviewers, I find that the main idea of this paper is extremely similar to [1], which also tries to solve the cross-domain gap by instance normalization, and restitution to handle the Reid task. Though they solve different tasks, the key idea is the same. As such, I degrade my score to reject.

[1] Style Normalization and Restitution for Generalizable Person Re-identification, in CVPR 20.
